name: Peroneal tendinopathy
populations: people with chronic lateral ankle instability
summary: Load-related pain and thickening of the peroneus brevis or longus tendon behind the lateral malleolus or at the cuboid groove. It is often linked to a cavovarus foot or lateral ankle instability.

keyFacts.label: Typical recovery
keyFacts.value: No trial data. Treatment is based on case series and expert opinion; most are managed non-operatively first

keyFacts.label: Return to sport
keyFacts.value: Criteria-based; no validated criteria. After surgery for tears, 46% returned to sport in one series

keyFacts.label: Key test
keyFacts.value: Pain on palpation of the tendons behind the lateral malleolus with resisted eversion or dorsiflexion; no accuracy data found

keyFacts.label: Imaging
keyFacts.value: Weight-bearing radiographs for foot shape, ultrasound for dynamic assessment, MRI for tears and associated lesions

keyFacts.label: Peak age
keyFacts.value: Active adults with repetitive loading; no reliable age data found

keyFacts.label: Incidence
keyFacts.value: True incidence unknown; frequently missed. Only 60% of 40 peroneal disorders were correctly diagnosed at first examination in one study cited in a review

overview:
The peroneus longus and brevis are the primary evertors of the foot and act as lateral ankle stabilisers. They are an under-appreciated source of lateral hindfoot pain that is easily mistaken for a lateral ankle ligament injury [r1]. Peroneal tendon disorders fall into three broad groups: tendinopathy and tenosynovitis, subluxation and dislocation, and splits and tears. They are often associated with ankle instability, hindfoot deformity and anomalous anatomy such as a low-lying peroneus brevis or a peroneus quartus [r1].

Peroneal tendinopathy is thought to result from overuse [r2]. The tendons run around the back of the lateral malleolus and under the cuboid, and both sites are exposed to compression and friction when load rises faster than the tendon can adapt [r1,r3]. Treatment recommendations are based mainly on case series and expert opinion [r1], so the evidence on this page is weaker than for tendinopathies such as the patellar and Achilles tendons. The load-based tendinopathy model offers a rational framework, but it has not been tested in peroneal tendons [r4,r5].

epidemiology.text: The true incidence of peroneal tendon pathology in clinical practice is unknown. Cadaveric studies suggest the prevalence of peroneus brevis tears is between 11% and 37%, with longus tears less frequent, and a retrospective MRI study suggested peroneal pathology in 35% of asymptomatic cases [r1]. Peroneal disorders are often missed: in one study, only 60% of 40 peroneal tendon disorders were accurately diagnosed at the first clinical evaluation, and acute dislocations are misdiagnosed in up to 40% of cases, usually as a lateral ankle sprain [r1]. Chronic disorders are common causes of posterolateral ankle pain and are often preceded by ligamentous instability or by predisposing anatomy such as a shallow fibular groove or a cavovarus foot [r3].

intrinsic: Cavovarus foot or hindfoot varus: in patients treated surgically for peroneal tendon tears the foot was cavovarus in 82% (a figure cited in a review), and most atraumatic cases have a varus heel [r1]
Chronic lateral ankle instability or a history of inversion injury [r1,r6]
Anatomical variants: a convex or flat retromalleolar groove, a prominent peroneal tubercle (over 5 mm), a low-lying peroneus brevis muscle belly or a peroneus quartus [r1,r6]
Os peroneum, which can entrap the longus tendon at the cuboid tunnel [r1,r6]
Heel valgus, for example from tibialis posterior insufficiency, which can trap the tendons between the fibular tip and the calcaneus [r1]
extrinsic: Prolonged, repetitive athletic activity, especially running and jumping [r1,r2]
A sudden rise in training load, hill or camber running (clinical reasoning; the load model predicts it, but no peroneal data were found) [r4]
Previous calcaneal fracture that widens the heel and crowds the tendons [r1]

mechanism.summary: Peroneal tendinopathy has no single injury moment. It develops when repetitive load, often with a supinated or varus foot and a lateral ankle that moves too much, exceeds the capacity of the tendons [r1,r2]. Both tendons turn around the back of the lateral malleolus in the retromalleolar groove, and the longus turns again under the cuboid. These turns concentrate compression and friction. Peroneal tendinopathy is likely to result from overuse, whereas subluxation more often follows forceful peroneal contraction during sudden dorsiflexion, for example landing or stopping abruptly [r2].
sequence: Training load or exposure rises, for example more running, hills, jumping or cutting, and the tendons are loaded in every stance phase.
A varus or cavus foot, or a lateral ankle that is unstable, makes the peroneals work harder to control inversion and keep the lateral column on the ground [r1].
The peroneals are the first muscles to contract in response to a sudden inversion stress, so they absorb many small perturbations [r1].
The tendons are compressed and rubbed at the retromalleolar groove, the peroneal tubercle and the cuboid tunnel [r1,r3].
Tendon cells and matrix react, the tendon thickens and the sheath becomes inflamed (tenosynovitis).
With continued load, the brevis tendon can become degenerate, split or tear, most often behind the malleolus, and the longus at the cuboid notch [r1].
Pain is felt behind and below the lateral malleolus, worst with activity and easing with rest [r1].

variants.name: Retromalleolar peroneus brevis tendinopathy
variants.description: Pain and swelling posterior to the fibula. It may be linked to a low-lying muscle belly, peroneus quartus, a flat groove or an unstable lateral ankle [r1,r6].

variants.name: Infrafibular and peroneal tubercle pain
variants.description: Pain along the lateral calcaneal wall, linked to a prominent peroneal tubercle (over 5 mm) that impinges the longus tendon, or to heel valgus [r1].

variants.name: Cuboid tunnel peroneus longus tendinopathy
variants.description: Plantar-lateral midfoot pain at the cuboid notch. It can be linked to an os peroneum (painful os peroneum syndrome) [r1].

variants.name: Acute-on-chronic after an ankle sprain
variants.description: An inversion injury strains tendons that are already irritated, or exposes a split tear. Pain at the back of the malleolus that persists after a sprain should prompt a peroneal assessment [r1].

anatomy.text: The peroneus brevis arises from the distal two-thirds of the fibula and becomes tendinous 2–3 cm above the fibular tip. The longus arises from the proximal two-thirds of the fibula and the lateral tibial condyle. Both are supplied by the superficial peroneal nerve. Together they lie in a common synovial sheath from about 4 cm above the tip of the lateral malleolus to 1 cm below it, within the retromalleolar groove, a fibro-osseous tunnel bounded by the superior peroneal retinaculum (SPR), the PTFL, the CFL and the PITFL [r1]. The brevis is flat and lies against the fibula, with the longus behind it. Below the groove the two tendons separate on either side of the peroneal tubercle: the brevis passes above it to the fifth metatarsal base, and the longus passes below it into the cuboid tunnel and then across the sole to the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform [r1]. The brevis provides about 63% of eversion power, and the longus plantarflexes the first ray [r1].

structures.name: Peroneus brevis tendon
structures.role: Everts the foot and is the main evertor; inserts on the fifth metatarsal base. It is the tendon most often torn [r1].

structures.name: Peroneus longus tendon
structures.role: Everts the foot and plantarflexes the first ray, stabilising the medial column. It passes under the cuboid [r1].

structures.name: Superior peroneal retinaculum (SPR)
structures.role: Primary restraint that holds the tendons in the retromalleolar groove. Failure causes subluxation or dislocation [r1].

structures.name: Retromalleolar groove and fibular malleolus
structures.role: A concave groove stabilises the tendons. In a cadaver study of 178 fibulae, it was concave in 82%, flat in 11% and convex in 7% [r1].

structures.name: Peroneal tubercle and cuboid tunnel
structures.role: Sites of impingement and friction for the longus tendon, particularly with a prominent tubercle or an os peroneum [r1].

structures.name: Lateral ankle ligaments (ATFL, CFL)
structures.role: Static restraint to inversion. Laxity increases the work of the peroneals [r1].

pathophysiology.tissueDamage:
Tendinopathy is a failure of the tendon to adapt to load, not simple inflammation. In the continuum model, a tendon moves through reactive tendinopathy, disrepair and degenerative stages. The early reactive stage can reverse with load management, but the late stage has fewer options. The model synthesises clinical and laboratory research and is itself debated: classifying a mainly painful condition by structure has been challenged, and the interplay between structure, pain and function is not fully understood [r4,r5]. These ideas come mostly from the patellar and Achilles tendons, and they have not been tested in peroneal tendons.

In the peroneals, the tendinopathy is typically thickening and focal degeneration, most often in the infra-malleolar portion, with nodular thickening, splits or tears [r1]. The brevis can split through attrition against the posterior fibula, or through compression between the fibula and the longus tendon in an inversion injury, and a split can follow or lead to subluxation [r1]. Vascularity may matter: three avascular zones were described that matched sites of tendinopathy, but their existence has been disputed [r1].

structures.name: Peroneus brevis tendon
structures.effect: Thickening, degeneration and sometimes a longitudinal split behind the lateral malleolus. Tears occurred in 88% of surgically treated cases in one cited series [r1].

structures.name: Peroneus longus tendon
structures.effect: Thickening or tear, most often at the cuboid notch or under the peroneal tubercle; less often torn than the brevis [r1].

structures.name: Tendon sheath
structures.effect: Tenosynovitis, with excess fluid around the tendons. Circumferential fluid wider than 3 mm in the common sheath is highly specific on MRI [r1].

structures.name: Superior peroneal retinaculum
structures.effect: Laxity or tear allows subluxation, which is a separate condition covered on another page [r1,r2].

structures.name: Lateral ankle ligaments and capsule
structures.effect: Laxity or previous sprain increases peroneal load. Tendinopathy can accompany chronic ankle instability [r1,r3].

structures.name: Sural and superficial peroneal nerves
structures.effect: Can be irritated by swelling or surgery (sural nerve irritation after injection or surgery was reported) [r7].

muscles.name: Peroneus longus and brevis muscles
muscles.effect: Overload and pain can reduce eversion strength. Weakness may also be a cause, because a varus heel may result from peroneal weakness as well as cause overload [r1].

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius and soleus
muscles.effect: Altered calf capacity and stiffness change loading through the lateral column (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Tibialis posterior and anterior
muscles.effect: The antagonists of the peronei. Imbalance influences the foot posture in stance (clinical reasoning).

muscles.name: Hip abductors and extensors
muscles.effect: Proximal control changes how the foot is placed on the ground (clinical reasoning).

cellular.description: After a load spike, tenocytes activate, proteoglycans increase and the tendon swells. The change can be reversible [r4].
Increased cell activity and matrix breakdown disorganise collagen, with new vessels and nerve ingrowth [r4].
Areas of cell death and disorganised matrix with limited capacity to reverse; splits and tears can develop [r4].

cellular.timing: About 12 weeks or more of progressive loading
cellular.description: Progressive loading builds tendon capacity and neuromuscular performance. The timescale comes from other tendons and has not been shown in the peroneals [r5].

systems.effect: Pain from the tendon, sheath and sensitised nerves limits activity. Peroneal reaction to a sudden inversion may be delayed after ankle sprain, but studies conflict [r1].
A cavovarus foot, hindfoot varus or a plantar-flexed first ray shifts load to the lateral column and the peroneals [r1].
The tendons receive blood through vincula; whether poorly vascularised zones explain the sites of tendinopathy is disputed [r1].
Systemic fluoroquinolone use is a recognised tendinopathy risk, but peroneal-specific data were not found (clinical reasoning).
Persistent pain, activity restriction and fear of damage are common in chronic tendinopathy (clinical reasoning).

grading.system: Anatomical classification of peroneal tendon disorders (no validated clinical grading)

grades.description: Pain, swelling and thickening of the tendons and sheath without a tear. The most common problem in athletes and the focus of this page [r1,r2].
grades.prognosis: Responds to non-operative treatment in many cases; refractory cases may need surgery [r1,r8]

grades.description: Tendons displace out of the retromalleolar groove; separate pathology covered on another page [r1,r2].
grades.prognosis: Non-operative treatment often fails in the acute and chronic stages; surgery is common [r1,r9]

grades.grade: Splits and tears (Brandes–Smith zones A, B, C)
grades.description: Zone A is under the superior retinaculum (subluxation, low-lying brevis or quartus), zone B is the inferior retinaculum and peroneal tubercle, and zone C is the cuboid notch [r1].
grades.prognosis: Surgery is based on how much viable tendon remains: tubularisation if under half the tendon is torn, and tenodesis if more [r8]

timeframes.summary: No natural-history or exercise-trial data were found for peroneal tendinopathy. The phases below follow the tendinopathy continuum model, and the time frames are clinical conventions taken from other tendons [r4,r5]. Criteria, not time, decide progression.

healing.description: Pain and swelling after a load spike. Reduce load and keep the tendon moving with isometric work.
Progressive isotonic strengthening of the evertors and the calf, with correction of contributing factors such as foot posture.
Heavy, slow single-leg loading and balance, with the load progression of tendon adaptation

healing.phase: Energy storage and return to sport
healing.description: Hopping, running progression and change of direction, with a return to full training

milestones.label: Start loaded evertor and calf strengthening
milestones.note: Once pain at rest is low and load is tolerated (clinical convention)

milestones.label: Return to running programme
milestones.note: Needs pain-free hopping and single-leg capacity (clinical convention)

milestones.label: Return to full sport
milestones.note: Often 3 to 6 months or longer for chronic cases (clinical convention); no validated criteria

timeframes.returnToSport: Criteria-based, with no validated criteria and no published time frame specific to non-operative treatment. After surgery for peroneal tendon tears, only 46% of 30 patients had returned to sport at an average of 31 months in one series [r10], while a review reports success rates of about 70–80% after tenodesis, with a return to activity at about 12 weeks [r1]. Expect a gradual return over months.

symptoms: Posterolateral ankle pain behind and below the lateral malleolus that worsens with activity and eases with rest [r1]
Swelling or a tender lump along the tendons behind the fibula or along the lateral calcaneal wall [r1]
Pain on push-off, running on a camber or uneven ground, and lateral ankle stiffness after rest
A feeling of lateral ankle weakness or instability, with or without a history of sprains [r3]
Snapping or popping (suggests subluxation or a split tear) and plantar-lateral midfoot pain at the cuboid [r1]
signs: Swelling posterior to the fibula or along the lateral wall of the calcaneus, with tenderness along the tendons [r1]
Pain with resisted eversion, passive inversion stretch or resisted plantarflexion of the first ray [r1]
A palpable mass that moves with the tendon, suggesting tendinosis [r1]
A cavus foot or hindfoot varus on standing [r1]
Signs of lateral ligament laxity on anterior drawer or talar tilt [r1]

subjective: Onset and course: gradual, load-related pain versus a sudden snap or a recent sprain [r1,r2]
Location: behind the malleolus, along the lateral heel, at the cuboid or at the fifth metatarsal base
Training: recent changes in volume, intensity, surface, footwear and hills or camber
Previous ankle sprains, giving way and any previous surgery [r1]
Snapping, popping or a feeling of tendons moving, which suggests subluxation or a split tear [r1]
Foot type and family history of high arches or neuromuscular disease (a varus heel can signal an underlying neuromuscular disorder) [r1]
Goals, sport and the time available before key events
observation: Standing and walking alignment, looking for cavus foot, hindfoot varus and a plantar-flexed first ray [r1]
Swelling behind the fibula and along the lateral calcaneus
Wasting of intrinsic foot muscles and clawing of lesser toes (neuromuscular screen) [r1]
palpation: Peroneal tendons in the retromalleolar groove, with resisted dorsiflexion and eversion [r1]
Tendons along the lateral calcaneal wall, over the peroneal tubercle, and under the cuboid
Base of the fifth metatarsal (brevis insertion) and the os peroneum region
Lateral ligaments (ATFL, CFL) and the lateral malleolus
Sural nerve course for neural tenderness
rangeOfMotion: Active and passive ankle and subtalar movement; pain on passive inversion stretch [r1]
Flexibility of any hindfoot varus, which determines whether orthoses can correct it [r1]
strength: Resisted eversion strength and pain, compared with the other side [r1]
Resisted first-ray plantarflexion for the longus [r1]
Single-leg heel raise capacity and endurance
Hip abductor and extensor strength (clinical reasoning)
neuro: Sensation over the lateral foot and dorsum (sural and superficial peroneal nerves)
Screen for peripheral neuropathy and neuromuscular disease when a varus heel is rigid or bilateral [r1]
functional: Single-leg stance and single-leg squat (eyes open, then closed)
Hop tests and change-of-direction when pain allows
Running gait assessment (foot strike, crossover and lateral loading; clinical reasoning)

specialTests.name: Palpation of the peroneal tendons with resisted dorsiflexion and eversion
specialTests.purpose: Localise pain to the peroneal tendons in the retromalleolar groove
specialTests.procedure: Palpate the tendons behind the fibula while the patient actively everts the foot against resistance, then add dorsiflexion. Compare with the other side.
specialTests.positive: Pain and tenderness along the tendons, with swelling or a nodule that moves with the tendon

specialTests.name: Resisted eversion and passive inversion stretch
specialTests.purpose: Provoke pain from the peroneal tendons and exclude other causes
specialTests.procedure: Resist eversion with the foot in slight plantarflexion. Then passively invert and plantarflex the foot to stretch the tendons.
specialTests.positive: Reproduction of lateral hindfoot pain; weakness suggests tear or inhibition

specialTests.name: Peroneal compression test (Sobel)
specialTests.purpose: Detect pain, crepitus or popping from the peroneals, and suggest subluxation or a split tear
specialTests.procedure: Apply pressure behind the distal fibula while the patient forcefully everts and dorsiflexes the ankle.
specialTests.positive: Pain, crepitus or a pop at the posterior edge of the distal fibula

specialTests.name: Active circumduction
specialTests.purpose: Screen for subluxation, which is a differential diagnosis
specialTests.procedure: Ask the patient to circumduct the ankle actively while you watch and feel behind the lateral malleolus.
specialTests.positive: Visible or palpable displacement of tendons over the fibular edge, snapping or pain

specialTests.name: Anterior drawer, talar tilt and standing hindfoot alignment
specialTests.purpose: Identify lateral ligament laxity and hindfoot varus as drivers of overload
specialTests.procedure: Test the lateral ligaments as in any ankle assessment. Then assess standing hindfoot alignment and whether the varus corrects (for example with a block under the lateral border).
specialTests.positive: Laxity of the ATFL or CFL, or a varus heel that does not correct

clinicalRules.name: No validated clinical rule or accuracy data found
clinicalRules.description: No sensitivity or specificity figures for the clinical tests were found in the sources read. Diagnosis rests on history, palpation and imaging, and in one study only 60% of 40 peroneal tendon disorders were diagnosed accurately at the first clinical evaluation [r1].

outcomeMeasures.name: Foot and Ankle Ability Measure (FAAM)
outcomeMeasures.use: Self-reported function in daily living and sport; track at each stage

outcomeMeasures.name: VISA-style pain scale or numeric pain rating after loading
outcomeMeasures.use: Monitor the load response over 24 hours (clinical convention)

outcomeMeasures.name: Single-leg heel raise to fatigue
outcomeMeasures.use: Tendon and calf capacity, compared with the other side

outcomeMeasures.name: Resisted eversion strength (handheld dynamometer or isometric hold)
outcomeMeasures.use: Evertor strength and pain; compare sides

outcomeMeasures.name: Cumberland Ankle Instability Tool (CAIT)
outcomeMeasures.use: Screen for the instability that often accompanies peroneal problems [r3]

imaging.modality: Weight-bearing radiographs of the ankle and foot
imaging.indication: Persistent lateral hindfoot pain or foot deformity
imaging.findings: Foot shape such as pes cavus, an enlarged peroneal tubercle, an os peroneum, bony spurs, and the 'fleck' sign of SPR avulsion [r1]

imaging.indication: Dynamic assessment of tendon thickness, splits and subluxation
imaging.findings: Real-time movement of tendons over the fibula, tendon thickening and sheath fluid. Accuracy for tendon tears was reported as 90% in one study cited in a review [r1].

imaging.indication: Suspected tear, persistent pain, or planning for surgery. It is the standard method of radiographic evaluation [r8].
imaging.findings: Tendinosis and tenosynovitis (increased signal and sheath fluid, with circumferential fluid wider than 3 mm highly specific), tears, a low-lying brevis or peroneus quartus, talar dome defects and subtalar disease. The 'magic angle' artefact reduces sensitivity and specificity to about 80% and 75% [r1].
Retromalleolar groove shape, a hypertrophied peroneal tubercle and lateral wall impingement after calcaneal fracture [r1]

differentials.name: Peroneal tendon subluxation or dislocation
differentials.distinguishing: Sudden onset after forceful dorsiflexion with peroneal contraction, snapping on circumduction or resisted eversion, and a retinaculum 'fleck' sign on radiograph [r1,r2]

differentials.name: Lateral ankle sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Clear inversion injury with ATFL or CFL tenderness. It often coexists with peroneal injury and can mask it.

differentials.name: Chronic ankle instability
differentials.distinguishing: Recurrent giving way and lateral laxity. It often drives peroneal overload [r1,r3].

differentials.name: Fifth metatarsal base fracture
differentials.distinguishing: Bony tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal after an inversion injury, which also gives peroneus brevis insertion pain

differentials.name: Osteochondral lesion of the talus
differentials.distinguishing: Deep ankle pain, catching or swelling that persists after a sprain; MRI confirms. It can coexist with peroneal tendon injury [r1].

differentials.name: High ankle (syndesmosis) sprain
differentials.distinguishing: Pain above the joint line, positive squeeze and external rotation tests, and an external rotation mechanism

differentials.name: Painful os peroneum syndrome
differentials.distinguishing: Plantar-lateral midfoot pain at the cuboid with an os peroneum that is fractured, enlarged or entrapped; radiograph or MRI shows it [r1]

differentials.name: Sinus tarsi syndrome and subtalar pathology
differentials.distinguishing: Pain in the lateral soft spot below the fibula with subtalar movement; MRI can show subtalar arthropathy [r1]

redFlags: A sudden pop with weakness of eversion or a palpable gap or loss of tendon contour: suspect a tendon rupture or an acute dislocation and arrange imaging and orthopaedic review [r1].
Recurrent snapping or tendons visibly displacing over the fibula: suspect subluxation. Non-operative treatment has high failure rates and surgery is often needed [r1,r9].
A recent inversion injury with bone tenderness at the malleoli or the fifth metatarsal base, or inability to take four steps: arrange radiographs to exclude fracture.
A rigid or bilateral varus heel, wasting of the intrinsic foot muscles, clawing of the toes or foot drop: screen for a neuromuscular disorder and refer for neurological assessment [r1].
Corticosteroid injection into the sheath carries a risk of tendon rupture, and some surgeons do not use it. If it is considered, it should be ultrasound-guided and decided by a specialist [r1,r7].

Failure to improve after about 3 months of properly loaded, supervised treatment (a clinical convention): refer for MRI and an orthopaedic opinion, because a split tear or other pathology may be present [r8].

management.principles: Treatment begins non-operatively. Recommendations rest on case series and expert opinion [r1], and no randomised trial of exercise for peroneal tendinopathy was found. The plan combines (1) load management of the reactive tendon, (2) progressive loading of the evertors and calf, and (3) correction of contributing factors such as a varus heel, lateral instability or training errors [r1,r4,r5]. The loading dosage is borrowed from patellar and Achilles tendinopathy, where eccentric loading has limited or conflicting advantage over other loading programmes and eccentric–concentric loading should be considered [r5]. Refractory cases, tears and subluxation need orthopaedic review [r1,r8].

medical.name: NSAIDs, relative rest and activity modification
medical.description: A review lists NSAIDs, rest, activity modification and orthoses as the first-line treatment of confirmed peroneal tendinosis [r1]. No trials were found, and NSAIDs should be short-term and approved by a clinician.

medical.name: Orthoses with lateral forefoot posting; correction of hindfoot varus
medical.description: A review describes orthoses with lateral forefoot posting in mild cases, and notes that flexibility of a varus heel affects orthotic management [r1]. Evidence is limited to expert opinion.

medical.name: Short-term immobilisation in a short-leg cast or walker boot
medical.description: In refractory cases a short-leg cast or controlled-ankle-movement walker for six weeks may be helpful, according to one review [r1]. It risks weakening the tendon and leg, so it is a last resort before surgery.

medical.name: Ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath
medical.description: In a retrospective case series of 96 patients (109 injections), 25% progressed to surgery, and 36.8% of 87 reporting had more than 12 weeks of relief while 43.7% had 0–1 weeks. There were 2 complications (1.8%), including one progression of a longus tear [r7]. A systematic review of tendon-sheath injections found low-quality studies and no placebo comparisons, and short-term pain improvement [r11]. Some surgeons avoid injection because of the risk of rupture [r1]. The evidence is conflicting and weak.

medical.name: Surgery (synovectomy, debridement, tubularisation or tenodesis)
medical.description: Operative treatment is reserved for failed non-operative care [r8]. Repair and tubularisation are used if less than half the tendon is torn, and tenodesis if more [r8]. Reported results vary: a review reports success of about 70–80% after tenodesis [r1], while one series found that only 46% of 30 patients returned to sport at an average of 31 months, with scar tenderness in 58% [r10].

physio.name: Load management and progressive tendon loading
physio.description: Reduce the aggravating load, keep the tendon moving, and then build load in stages by pain response, from isometric to isotonic to heavy slow and then energy-storage work. The model comes from other tendinopathies, where eccentric-only loading is not clearly better than other programmes [r5,r4]. There is no peroneal-specific trial.

physio.name: Evertor and calf strengthening with single-leg and balance progression
physio.description: Strengthen the peroneals and the calf complex and train single-leg control, because the peroneals are the first muscles to respond to a sudden inversion and are the dynamic stabilisers of the lateral ankle [r1]. Dosages are conventions.

physio.name: Assessment and correction of contributing factors
physio.description: Check foot posture (cavus or varus), lateral ligament laxity, footwear and training load. Treat associated lateral instability with the usual sensorimotor and strength program [r1,r3].

physio.name: Taping or bracing for lateral instability
physio.description: If lateral ankle instability drives the problem, an external support during sport can reduce the load on the peroneals (clinical reasoning). No peroneal-specific data were found.

physio.name: Prolonged complete rest or immobilisation
physio.description: Rest settles the reactive tendon but does not build capacity. Long immobilisation without loading is expected to leave the tendon and the muscle weaker (clinical reasoning); the review keeps cast immobilisation for refractory cases [r1].

education: Peroneal tendon pain is a load problem. It usually settles with the right amount of loading and with attention to foot posture and ankle stability, not just rest.
Do not stop all activity. Keep the tendon moving and work with your physio to find a load you can repeat without pain flaring the next day.
Recovery takes months for many people. Treatment advice is based on case series and expert opinion, so progress should be judged by your own response.
If the tendon snaps, pops or gives way, or you cannot push off, tell your physio, because you may have a tear or subluxation.
Footwear and the way your foot lands can add to the load, so bring your running shoes to your appointment.

rehab.overview: No trial has tested a rehabilitation programme for peroneal tendinopathy, so this programme follows the tendinopathy load model borrowed from other tendons [r4,r5]. Progression is criteria-based and driven by the pain response at the tendon: an acceptable symptom response is mild pain that settles within 24 hours (a clinical convention). Time frames are typical ranges and dosages are common clinical conventions, not trial doses. If a split tear or subluxation is suspected, the programme should be modified after specialist assessment.

stages.name: Settle the reactive tendon
goals: Reduce load to a tolerable level
Maintain tendon movement and strength with isometrics
Address obvious contributors such as footwear and a varus heel
precautions: Exclude fracture, acute rupture and subluxation first (red flags)
Avoid sudden increases in running, jumping and cutting
No stretching of the peroneals into forced inversion

exercises.name: Isometric eversion hold (against a wall or a band)
exercises.cues: Press the outer foot into the wall without moving the ankle

exercises.name: Ankle alphabet (pain-free)
exercises.cues: Move from the ankle in a small, comfortable range

exercises.name: Double-leg calf raise
exercises.dosage: 2 × 10, slow, once daily if pain allows
exercises.cues: Rise evenly over both big toes, avoid rolling out

exercises.name: Cycling or pool work
exercises.cues: Easy effort, pain 3/10 or less

exercises.name: Single-leg balance
exercises.cues: Soft knee, stay tall, keep the arch lifted

progressionCriteria: Morning and daily pain 3/10 or less
Isometric eversion tolerated with mild or no pain

stages.name: Progressive strength
precautions: Increase load only if the 24-hour response is acceptable
Do not stretch into forced inversion or end-range eversion with load
Use tape, brace or orthoses if they reduce pain

exercises.name: Band-resisted eversion (isotonic)
exercises.dosage: 3 × 15, 3 s up and 3 s down, daily, increasing band resistance
exercises.cues: Move only the ankle, control the return

exercises.name: Single-leg calf raise (progress from double-leg)
exercises.cues: Rise over the big toe, avoid rolling out

exercises.name: Single-leg balance on a soft surface
exercises.cues: Quiet ankle, level hips

exercises.name: Step-ups and controlled step-downs
exercises.cues: Knee over the second toe, control the lowering

exercises.name: Hip abductor and extensor strengthening
exercises.cues: Level pelvis, no trunk lean

progressionCriteria: 10 single-leg calf raises with an acceptable pain response
Band eversion 3 × 15 at moderate resistance without a flare
Pain at the tendon 2/10 or less in daily life

stages.name: Heavy, slow and single-leg loading
goals: Build high tendon and muscle capacity
Single-leg strength and control through the whole chain
precautions: Keep progressions gradual and review after each increase
Stop and re-assess if pain stays above 4/10 or does not settle in 24 hours
Limit sudden direction changes and hills until this stage is complete

exercises.name: Weighted single-leg calf raise
exercises.dosage: 4 × 6–10 with a dumbbell, 3 s up and 3 s down, 2–3 times per week
exercises.cues: Drive over the big toe, no rolling out

exercises.name: Heavy resisted eversion (cable or heavy band)
exercises.cues: Slow tempo, full range within comfort

exercises.name: Single-leg squat to a chair
exercises.cues: Level pelvis, knee over the second toe

exercises.name: Lateral step-down and lateral lunge
exercises.cues: Hips back, foot flat, no collapse into the outer border

exercises.name: Walk–jog progression
exercises.dosage: 1 min jog, 1 min walk, 8–10 rounds, building jog time every 2–3 sessions
exercises.cues: Short, quiet steps under the body, avoid running on a camber

progressionCriteria: Single-leg calf raise 15 repetitions or more with load, close to the other side (clinical convention)
Jogging 20 minutes with an acceptable response
Resisted eversion strength within about 10% of the other side (clinical convention)

stages.name: Energy storage, change of direction and return to sport
goals: Change of direction and sport-specific drills
precautions: Progress hopping and cutting in volume before intensity
Keep tape, brace or orthoses if they help in sport
Re-assess if swelling or snapping returns

exercises.name: Double-leg then single-leg hopping
exercises.dosage: 3 × 8 double-leg, then 3 × 5 single-leg hops with a 2 s stick, 2–3 times per week
exercises.cues: Soft landing, ankle, knee and hip bend together

exercises.name: Landing and deceleration drills
exercises.cues: Land on the full foot, not the outer border

exercises.name: Planned then reactive change-of-direction drills
exercises.dosage: 2–3 sessions per week, progressing speed and angle
exercises.cues: Lower the centre of mass, plant the foot under the knee

exercises.name: Running progression on varied surfaces
exercises.dosage: Build volume by about 10% per week (a clinical convention)
exercises.cues: Quiet foot strike, avoid heavy outer-border loading

exercises.name: Maintenance loading
exercises.dosage: Weighted single-leg calf raise and band eversion, 1–2 times per week long term
exercises.cues: Keep the strength you gained

progressionCriteria: Hop tests within about 90% of the other leg without pain (clinical convention)
Full training volume with no next-day flare
Confidence and readiness rated high by the athlete

criteria: No validated return-to-sport criteria exist for peroneal tendinopathy. These are common clinical conventions.
No pain or swelling along the tendons at rest or after a full training session, and no next-day flare
Pain-free palpation, resisted eversion and single-leg heel raise to fatigue
Eversion and calf strength within about 10% of the other side (clinical convention)
Hop and change-of-direction tests without pain, giving way, or snapping
Contributing factors (foot posture, footwear, lateral instability and training load) addressed
Running or sport volume rebuilt gradually with a plan for tape, brace or orthoses if used
tests: Single, triple and side hop tests

prognosis: No natural-history data or controlled trials of non-operative care were found, so the outlook is uncertain. Reviews state that these conditions generally respond to non-operative treatment such as physiotherapy, NSAIDs and immobilisation, and that untreated disorders can lead to persistent lateral ankle pain and substantial functional problems [r1]. Tenosynovitis typically responds to conservative therapy, with surgery reserved for refractory cases [r8]. After surgery, outcomes vary: a review reports success rates of about 70–80% after tenodesis, with return to activity at about 12 weeks [r1], while one series of 30 patients found that nine of 10 returned to work but only 46% returned to sport at an average of 31 months, with residual scar tenderness in 58% and lateral swelling in 54% [r10]. A common underlying cause (cavovarus foot or lateral instability) that is not treated may lead to recurrence (clinical reasoning).
prevention: There is no peroneal-specific prevention trial. The recommendations below come from tendon load principles and clinical reasoning [r4,r5].
Increase running, jumping and hill volume gradually, and allow recovery between hard sessions (clinical convention).
Treat ankle instability and cavovarus foot posture early, because they are frequent companions of peroneal tendon disorders [r1,r3].
Maintain evertor, calf and balance strength after a sprain, rather than stopping at pain resolution (clinical reasoning).
Review footwear, and avoid prolonged running on cambered surfaces (clinical reasoning).
clinicalPearls: Lateral ankle pain after a 'sprain' that does not settle may be peroneal. Palpate the tendons behind the fibula during resisted eversion and dorsiflexion before you call it a slow sprain [r1].
Look at the foot as well as the tendon. Most atraumatic cases have a varus heel, and 82% of operatively treated tears occurred in cavovarus feet in one cited series [r1].
Test the lateral ligaments. Instability and peroneal tendon pain often coexist [r1,r3].
Ask about snapping. Snapping or popping behind the malleolus points to subluxation or a split tear and changes the plan [r1].
Be honest about the evidence: there are no peroneal exercise trials, and the loading programme is borrowed from other tendons [r5].
Be cautious about corticosteroid injection: the case-series data are weak, some surgeons avoid it, and rupture is a recognised risk [r1,r7].

forces.label: Peroneals work to control the foot

captions.text: A runner steps up weekly distance and adds hills and cambered roads.
Every stance phase loads the peroneal tendons behind the lateral malleolus.
A varus foot or a lateral ankle that moves too much makes the peroneals work harder to control inversion.
Healthy tendons adapt if load builds gradually and recovery is long enough.
When load rises faster than the tendon's capacity, the tendon becomes painful.
There is no single injury moment: pain builds up behind and below the ankle bone.
Zooming into the right ankle from the side.
The peroneus brevis and longus run together behind the lateral malleolus.
Here the tendons turn a corner, so compression and friction are highest.
With repeated overload, the tendon and its sheath become irritated and swollen.
Pain is felt behind and below the ankle bone, and is worse with activity.
The tendon thickens and becomes disorganised. It degenerates; it does not usually rupture.
Over time, the brevis can split. A split tear and a subluxation are separate problems to check for.
Healthy tendon: tightly packed, aligned type I collagen with a few resident tenocytes.
Reactive: after a load spike, tenocytes activate and the matrix swells. This can reverse.
Disrepair: cells try to repair the tendon, the collagen becomes disorganised and new vessels appear.
Degenerative: areas of cell death and disorganised matrix remain, with less capacity to reverse.
Progressive loading builds capacity and tendon pain can settle as the tendon adapts.
